# Diagnosing Intermittent Hissing in a Post-Evaporator Swap on a Mitsubishi Outlander

Replacing an evaporator is a significant service for any vehicle, particularly a 2016 Mitsubishi Outlander where access can be tight and the new unit often requires careful handling to avoid crushing the copper lines. Once the job is done and the system is evacuated, you might expect immediate silence or just the standard hum of the compressor and blower. However, if you are hearing an intermittent hissing sound from the AC vent that appears only when the system is cooling and vanishes when switched to fan-only mode, the issue likely lies within the refrigerant charge or a restriction in the low-pressure side.

The fact that the hissing stops completely when you switch the climate control to "Fan" mode is the critical diagnostic clue here. In fan-only mode, the compressor is disengaged. The compressor is the primary driver of pressure differentials within the system; without it moving refrigerant, there is no suction or high side pressure to force gas through any leaks or restrictions. Therefore, this symptom confirms that the source of the noise is directly tied to the active compression cycle and the flow dynamics of the refrigerant, not an electrical fault in the blower motor or a mechanical issue within the cabin air box itself.

When you observe a hissing sound coming and going intermittently while cooling, you are almost certainly listening to escaping high-pressure gas. This can happen for two main reasons: a residual leak at the service ports or a restriction downstream of the new evaporator. Even though the technician evacuated the system, small leaks at the flare nuts connecting the condenser to the receiver-drier (or accumulator) can allow refrigerant to escape. As the compressor pumps gas into the low side, it rushes out through these tiny gaps, creating that distinct hiss. The fact that it starts and stops suggests the pressure differential is fluctuating as the system cycles between high and low load conditions, or perhaps a valve on the new evaporator is not seating perfectly due to debris left in the line during the swap.

Another possibility specific to recent evaporator replacements is a restriction in the liquid line immediately after the receiver-drier. If there was any particulate matter dislodged from the old unit or if the new o-ring was installed incorrectly, it could create a partial blockage. As refrigerant tries to pass through this restriction, it can accelerate and escape past the seal of the restrictor plate or a micro-leak in the fitting, generating noise. The intermittent nature often correlates with the thermal expansion of the lines; as the system heats up during operation, metal expands, potentially tightening a loose fitting enough to stop the leak, only for it to hiss again as pressure builds and components settle back into place.

To resolve this, you must verify the refrigerant charge level first. If the system is undercharged, the compressor will run harder to maintain pressure, exacerbating any minor leaks. Using manifold gauges, check the low-side pressure while the AC is running at maximum cooling. If the pressure drops significantly faster than expected or reads below the saturation point for the given temperature, a leak is confirmed. You will need to locate the source using an electronic leak detector and repair it before recharging.

If the charge is correct and no external leaks are found, inspect the service port adapters on the new evaporator lines. Ensure the flare nuts are torqued to the manufacturer's specification; overtightening can distort the aluminum flange, while undertightening leaves a gap for gas to escape. Once any leaks are sealed or restrictions cleared, evacuate the system to ensure no air remains, then recharge with the exact amount of R-134a specified in the service manual. If the noise persists after these steps, further inspection of the internal valves on the new evaporator assembly may be required to rule out a manufacturing defect in the component itself.
